newsitem.title: GERMANY: DURUM SHORTAGE RAISES PROCESSING COSTS IN GERMANY.
newsitem.headline: DURUM SHORTAGE RAISES PROCESSING COSTS IN GERMANY.

text.p: German durum wheat millers are likely to suffer raw material shortages from generally lower harvests and may need to pass on higher prices to consumers in the pasta manufacturing industry, a leading miller said on Monday.
"The European Union may need eight million tonnes of durum this year but the EU harvest will bring six million at best," said Frank Lorenz of Mannheim-based Hildebrandmuehlen.
Lorenz heads the association of 23 major German durum wheat mills and was elaborating on joint statements from mills and pasta makers warning of price rises.
"Most of the additional volume will have to come from Canada, where there will be severe drought losses," he said.
"The problem is compounded by crop losses in North Africa, which will compete in import markets with the EU."
Lorenz, who also cited dollar firmness, said latest millers' buying-in prices for the winter season were 40 percent above the average in the first six months of 1997.
Durum wheat accounts for roughly 20 to 40 percent of premium pasta production costs.
Lorenz said his association was lobbying Brussels to review a reduction in the durum wheat area under the 1990 EU farm reform.
This package had squeezed out producers in the north of Europe to the benefit of southern member states.
"This policy needs to change because it bunches climatic crop risks, drives up the internal price and makes the EU overly dependent on imports," he said.
The EU had agreed high and permanent subsidies to durum growers.
The subsidies were paid out in October, which encouraged producers to hoard grain and push prices higher.
Millers of durum wheat and producers of semolina had asked Brussels for an expansion of EU durum areas and for a rescheduling of subsidy pay-outs until the spring.
EU pasta production was rising by five percent each year due to higher domestic use and export gains.
The International Grain Council (IGC) in its July report put world durum output in 1997 at less than 29 million tonnes, about five million down from 1996.
